title: Proposal
text:
This project proposes the development of a machine learning (ML) based classification of Sheffield neighbourhoods according to their transport environment characteristics. Using publicly available transport, demographic, socio-economic and environmental data, the study will identify groups of neighbourhoods that share similar characteristics.
The resulting typology will provide a common evidence base for transport planning, regeneration, climate policy, public health interventions and place-based decision making. Rather than predicting an outcome, the project applies unsupervised machine learning techniques to discover naturally occurring neighbourhood types.

title: Proposal
text:
2.1 Problem Statement
Sheffield possesses a wide range of datasets covering road networks, traffic flows, speed restrictions, population characteristics, employment patterns, and socio-economic factors. However, these datasets are typically analysed separately, making it difficult to understand how neighbourhood transport environments vary across the city.
Questions include:

Which areas have similar transport characteristics?
Where is car dependency greatest?
Which neighbourhoods experience transport accessibility challenges?
How should transport policies vary between different types of places?

Currently, no consistent city-wide transport environment classification exists to support strategic decision-making.

title: Proposal
text:
2.2 Aim

To develop an evidence-based classification of Sheffield neighbourhoods that groups areas with similar transport, accessibility and socio-economic characteristics into meaningful transport environment types.

The working title is Neighbourhood Transport Environment Typology (NTET).
The council has previously used similar geodemographic classification products called Acorn and Mosaic. All three answer the same broad question i.e. “what kind of place is this?” The difference is the lens through which they classify places. Acorn and Mosaic classify people and places for marketing and service design, whereas NTET will classify neighbourhoods for transport planning and policy design.







System
Primary focus




Acorn
Consumer and socio-economic characteristics of residents


Mosaic
Consumer, lifestyle and behavioural segmentation


NTET
Transport, accessibility, mobility and built-environment characteristics

title: Proposal
text:
2.3 Research Question

Can Sheffield neighbourhoods be classified into a small number of meaningful transport environment types that improve understanding, comparison and targeting of transport policies and interventions?

title: Proposal
text:
2.4 Objectives

Create a neighbourhood-level analytical dataset.

Examine relationships between transport, demographic and socio-economic indicators.

Identify groups of neighbourhoods using clustering algorithms.

Evaluate cluster robustness and interpretability.

Produce a practical transport environment typology.

Assess potential applications within local government decision-making.

title: Proposal
text:
3.1 Study Geography
The preferred unit of analysis is the 343 Lower Super Output Areas (LSOA), providing a balance between geographical detail and interpretability.
Alternative Sheffield geographies are neighbourhoods (100), MSOAs (70), or Wards (28).

title: Proposal
text:
3.2 Stage 1: Data Preparation

Assemble datasets
Handle missing values
Standardise variables
Explore distributions
Examine correlations

title: Proposal
text:
3.3 Stage 2: Exploratory Analysis
Use exploratory techniques to understand the principal dimensions of variation across neighbourhoods, including correlation analysis and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
Potential latent dimensions may include:

Urban intensity
Accessibility
Connectivity
Car dependency

Note: “Potential latent dimensions” refer to underlying neighbourhood characteristics that are not directly measured but may be inferred from correlations among observed variables. PCA will be used to identify these underlying dimensions and assess whether they represent concepts such as urban intensity, accessibility, connectivity, or car dependency.

title: Proposal
text:
3.4 Stage 3: Clustering approaches compared
K-Means: simple implementation, easily explained to non-technical audiences, and computationally efficient.
Hierarchical Clustering: produces a hierarchy of neighbourhood relationships and useful for interpretation.
Gaussian Mixture Models: allows probabilistic cluster membership and captures uncertainty in classification.

title: Proposal
text:
3.5 Stage 4: Cluster evaluation

Silhouette score
Cluster stability
Statistical separation
Policy interpretability

The preferred solution will balance statistical performance with practical usefulness.

title: Proposal
text:
4.1 NTET Pros & Cons







Advantages
Disadvantages




Holistic view of place: Reflects the reality that road safety, accessibility, public health, active travel and sustainability are all influenced by the same underlying transport environment.
Risk of becoming too broad: A classification designed to support many objectives may not be optimal for any single objective.


Supports place-based decision making: Enables neighbourhoods to be understood as complete transport environments rather than through individual datasets or performance indicators.
Loss of specificity: Important distinctions relevant to road safety or accessibility may be masked when multiple objectives are combined into a single typology.


Improves communication: Provides a simple and intuitive framework, similar to Acorn or Mosaic, that is easier for senior leaders and non-specialists to understand.
Harder to interpret: Cluster membership may be driven by several factors at once, making it difficult to explain why a neighbourhood belongs to a particular type.


Encourages integrated policy: Helps identify interventions that can deliver multiple benefits, such as improved safety, healthier travel choices and better accessibility.
Hidden weighting issues: Some themes may dominate the classification simply because they contribute more variables than others.


Creates a shared evidence base: Can be used across transport planning, public health, regeneration, climate and economic development activities.
More difficult to validate: There is no single outcome against which the typology can be tested, unlike a dedicated safety or accessibility model.


Reusable analytical asset: The classification could support future modelling, strategy development and investment prioritisation.
Potential stakeholder disagreement: Different service areas may have different views about which objectives and variables should be included.


Identifies underlying transport environments: Can reveal that geographically distant neighbourhoods share similar transport challenges and opportunities.
Risk of mission creep: Additional objectives can continually be added, increasing complexity and reducing clarity.

title: Proposal
text:
4.3 Illustrative Typology
Potential neighbourhood categories may include:

Connected Urban Centres with high employment density, excellent accessibility, strong public transport provision, and lower reliance on private cars.

Mixed Urban Neighbourhoods with medium density, moderate accessibility, and diverse travel behaviours.

Car-Oriented Outer Suburbs with lower density, greater car dependency, and longer travel distances.

Industrial and Employment Areas with a high concentration of jobs, strategic road access, and limited residential population.

Peripheral Communities with lower accessibility, potential transport poverty concerns, and greater travel challenges.

Final categories would emerge from the data-driven modelling process.

title: Proposal
text:
4.4 Potential Applications
Transport Strategy: support development of location-specific transport policies.
Active Travel: identify neighbourhoods with high potential for walking and cycling interventions.
Public Health: investigate relationships between transport environments and health outcomes.
Climate and Sustainability: identify areas where modal shift opportunities may be greatest.
Regeneration: support understanding of how transport conditions align with economic development priorities.
Future Predictive Analytics: provide contextual features for future transport, demand forecasting and road-safety models.

title: Proposal
text:
4.5 Benefits
Technical:

Demonstrates unsupervised machine learning capability.
Produces reusable analytical assets.
Strengthens spatial data science capability.

Organisational:

Creates a shared evidence base.
Improves understanding of neighbourhood transport environments.
Supports place-based policy design.

Academic:

Applies machine learning to a real organisational challenge.
Demonstrates feature engineering, clustering and model evaluation.
Meets the requirements of a business-focused machine learning project.

title: Proposal
text:
4.6 Future Development
Potential follow-on work includes:

Comparing outcomes across neighbourhood types.
Incorporating typology classifications into predictive models.
Supporting investment prioritisation and policy targeting.

This would create a reusable analytical framework that complements future transport and road-safety modelling projects.

title: Neighbourhood Transport Environment Typology
text:
The Neighbourhood Transport Environment Typology (NTET) will provide a common evidence base for transport planning, regeneration, climate policy, and public health interventions across the city.



For example:
LSOA     NTET Group
Area A    Car-Dependent Suburb
Area B    Car-Dependent Suburb
Area C    Industrial Employment Hub
Area D    Peripheral Community


Main deliverables:
 
a) A city-wide map showing the transport type of every neighbourhood (343 LSOAs).
b) A profile describing each type.
c) Statistics showing how neighbourhoods differ across the types.



NTET is a simplification tool, it allows a stakeholder to move from analysing hundreds of neighbourhoods individually to understanding a handful of meaningful place types. Instead of asking “What transport intervention does every LSOA need?”, they can ask “What interventions work best for Car-Dependent Suburbs?” or “Which Peripheral Communities have similar accessibility challenges?”. NTET allows neighbourhoods to be compared with genuinely similar places rather than against city-wide averages.
The council has previously paid to use similar geodemographic segmentation products called Acorn and Mosaic. All three answer the same broad question i.e. “What kind of place is this?” The difference is the lens through which they classify places. Acorn and Mosaic classify people and places for marketing and service design, whereas NTET classifies neighbourhoods for transport planning and policy design.
A practical example could be how to prioritise cycling investment. Without NTET we would review each neighbourhood individually, create bespoke analysis for each area, and it would be difficult to compare places consistently. With NTET we identify which transport environment types have low cycling infrastructure and short trip patterns, target those classes first, and can assess whether interventions work differently by neighbourhood type.
NTET is not intended to be an end product. It will be an analytical asset that can be reused across multiple projects.
A secondary, but potentially equally valuable use, is that NTET could become a foundational dataset used in future models. For example, EV charging planning, or climate and decarbonisation work.
In summary: NTET is a city-wide classification of neighbourhoods, similar to Acorn or Mosaic, but focused on transport. It provides a common framework used to compare similar places, target interventions, benchmark outcomes, and support future analytical models.

title: Exploratory Analysis for Clustering
text:
Before we look at applying a clustering algorithm, it’s useful to explore the candidate variables. Unlike supervised learning, clustering has no outcome variable, so exploratory analysis focuses on understanding the structure of the feature space. The objectives are to identify missing values, examine variable distributions, detect highly correlated features, identify potential transformations, and ensure that no single concept is disproportionately represented in the clustering algorithm. TODO: add ref??
Exploratory analysis is a standard part of clustering workflows because clustering algorithms are sensitive to the representation of the feature space. Examining variable distributions, identifying outliers, assessing correlations between variables, and applying appropriate transformations and standardisation can improve the interprability and stability of cluster solutions (Tan, Steinbach & Kumar, 2019; Kaufman & Rousseeuw, 2005).
In predictive modelling you often ask: Does this variable improve prediction?
In clustering we ask: Does this variable help distinguish meaningful neighbourhood types?

  st_transform(4326) |>
  left_join(df_lsoa |> select(LSOA21CD, cycle_infra_length_m), by = "LSOA21CD") |>

    fill_colour = if_else(has_cycle, "#2166ac", "#ff964f")

  fitBounds(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]], bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymax"]]) |>
  addPolygons(
    data        = sf_lsoa_cycle_infra,
    fillColor   = ~fill_colour,
    fillOpacity = 0.6,
    color       = "white",
    weight      = 0.5,
    smoothFactor = 0.5
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "topright",
    colors   = c("#2166ac", "#ff964f"),
    labels   = c(
      "Some recorded cycling infrastrcuture", 
      "No recorded cycling infrastructure"
    ),
    opacity  = 0.6,
    title    = NULL
  )




Figure 4: LSOAs with and without recorded cycling infrastructure








We were careful to include the term “recorded” alongside cycling infrastructure. From local, rather than subject-matter-expert, knowledge there was a suspicion of a gap between “recorded” by OS and actual. To include recorded cycling infrastructure in our model we first needed to do some investigatory work. Even if we were to take “recorded” at face value, the high proportion of zero values means that the variable contributes very little to distinguishing between most neighbourhoods. Nevertheless, it could be a key distinction.
It turn out that what we’ve defined as “cycling infrastructure” is more the issue rather than what’s been “recorded” by OS. We’ve attempted to define it as segregated provision, with physical separation from traffic via a kerb, bollards, grade separation etc., with higher perceived and actual safety. This is instead of also including on-road provision i.e. paint only and cyclists mix with traffic with low level of protection. We’ve derived our cycling infrastructure variable from the OS NGD transport schema where “highway dedication” generally refers to the legal rights associated with a route, not the physical design. What we have is “routes specifically available to cyclists away from the ordinary highway network”, rather than “engineered cycling infrastructure”. At the very least we should describe the variable as “designated cycle tracks, cycle ways and bridleways per LSOA derived from OS NGD Highway Dedication data”, rather than “cycling infrastructure” without qualification.
The following map highlights the inadequacy of our current definition and therefore the variable.


Code
# Same definition used in target to get the numbers 
sf_cycle_track <- sf_ngd_highway |>
  filter(description %in% c("Cycle Track Or Cycle Way", "Bridleway")) |> 
  st_transform(4326)

bb <- sf_cycle_track |> st_bbox()

make_basemap() |>
  fitBounds(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]], bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymax"]]) |>
  addPolygons(
    data = sf_city |> st_transform(4326),
    color = "black",
    fillOpacity = 0
  ) |> 
  addPolylines(
    data = sf_cycle_track,
    color = "red",
    weight = 4,
    smoothFactor = 0.5,
    opacity = 1
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "topright",
    colors   = c("red", "black"),
    labels   = c(
      "Cycle track",
      "City boundary"

Having acquired our data (ETL) and spent some time understanding it (EDA), this page will employ clustering algorithms.
We’re using the {tidymodels}1 framework, a collection of R packages for machine learning. In particular, we’re using the {tidyclust}2 R package, which is effectively a clustering specific replacement for the {tidymodels} package {parsnip}3.

title: Output Area Classification
text:
Code
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(targets)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(writexl)

# Sources all R/*.R same as _targets.R
tar_source()       

# Objects needed from our {targets} pipeline
tar_load(sf_lsoa)
tar_load(df_lsoa_ward)
tar_load(file_oac)
tar_load(file_oac_names)

# ggplot theme
set_theme(theme_minimal())
This is a brief exploration of the Output Area Classifications1 (OAC), hosted by the Geographic Data Service2 (March 2021 to March 2022).
OAC doesn’t have the “transport lens” that NTET intends. However, unlike the Acorn and Mosaic products, OAC is openly available allowing us to explore how NTET might look and operate. NTET is not expected to be hierarchical and will probably only have around half a dozen classifications, so something akin to the eight OAC Supergroups. The OAC classifications are arguably more intuitive for Local Government evidence-based policy making than Acorn or Mosaic. However, the OAC is four years old and a lot of the value of the Acorn and Mosaic products is in the additional underlying data sources, and currency of that data and their product releases.
The OAC is “a hierarchical geodemographic classification which identifies neighbourhoods across the UK that share similar characteristics. The taxonomy classifies Output Areas (OAs) into 8 different Supergroups, along with 21 nested Groups and 52 nested Subgroups”. The OAC for England and Wales is for each LSOA. It is built using official government statistical estimates and the classification methodology is the subject of an academic paper3.
Code
# **** Read OAC files ****

# File with classifications for all UK LSOAs
df_oac_all <- read_csv(file_oac)

# File with names for different classification codes
df_oac_names <- read_csv(file_oac_names)

# Only interested in Sheffield LSOA classifications
sf_oac <- sf_lsoa |> 
  left_join(df_oac_all, join_by(LSOA21CD == geography_code))

# **** Work towards a wide data set of classification code and names ****

df_oac_names_subgroup <- df_oac_names |> 
  filter(Level == "Subgroup") |> 
  mutate(
    supergroup_code = str_sub(`Classification Code`, 1, 1),
    group_code = str_sub(`Classification Code`, 1, 2)
  ) |> 
  select(
    supergroup_code,
    group_code,
    subgroup_code = `Classification Code`,
    subgroup_name = `Classification Name`
  )

df_oac_names_group <- df_oac_names |> 
  filter(Level == "Group") |> 
  select(
    group_code = "Classification Code",
    group_name = "Classification Name"
  )

df_oac_names_supergroup <- df_oac_names |> 
  filter(Level == "Supergroup") |> 
  select(
    supergroup_code = "Classification Code",
    supergroup_name = "Classification Name"
  )

df_oac_names_wide <- df_oac_names_subgroup |> 
  left_join(df_oac_names_group, join_by(group_code)) |> 
  left_join(df_oac_names_supergroup, join_by(supergroup_code)) |> 
  relocate(group_name, .after = group_code) |> 
  relocate(supergroup_name, .after = supergroup_code)

# Add the classification names to Sheffield LSOA classifications
sf_oac <- sf_oac |> 
  left_join(df_oac_names_wide, join_by(Subgroup == subgroup_code))

# Add wards
sf_oac <- sf_oac |> 
  left_join(
    select(df_lsoa_ward, LSOA21CD, WD25CD, WD25NM), 
    join_by(LSOA21CD)
  ) |> 
  rename(subgroup_code = Subgroup) |> 
  select(-Group, -Supergroup)

# No spatial list
df_oac <- sf_oac |> 
  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  select(
    LSOA21CD,
    LSOA21NM,
    WD25CD,
    WD25NM,
    supergroup_code,
    supergroup_name,
    group_code,
    group_name,
    subgroup_code,
    subgroup_name
  )

# Table of 6 random records
set.seed(123)
df_oac |> 
  slice_sample(n = 6) |> 
  my_gt() |> 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#D9EAD3"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = 1:2)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#93C47D"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = 3:4)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#DCEAF7"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = 5:6)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#B6D7F0"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = 7:8)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#6FA8DC"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = 9:10)
  )

Code
# Re-project for leaflet
sf_oac <- sf_oac |> 
  st_transform(4326) |> 
  mutate(supergroup_code = as.integer(supergroup_code))

# Palettes
pal_sg  <- colorNumeric(palette = "Oranges", domain = sf_oac$supergroup_code)
pal_grp <- colorFactor(
  palette = colorRampPalette(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(12, "Paired"))(20),
  domain  = sf_oac$group_code
)

# Bounding box
bb <- sf_oac |> st_bbox()

# Legend label lookups
sg_lookup <- sf_oac |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(supergroup_code, supergroup_name) |>
  arrange(supergroup_code) |>
  mutate(label = paste(supergroup_code, supergroup_name, sep = ". "))

grp_lookup <- sf_oac |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(group_code, group_name) |>
  arrange(group_code) |>
  mutate(label = paste(group_code, group_name, sep = " - "))

# Shared popup
popup_html <- ~paste0(
  "<b>", LSOA21CD, "</b> ", LSOA21NM, "<br>",
  "<b>Supergroup:</b> ", supergroup_code, " - ", supergroup_name, "<br>",
  "<b>Group:</b> ", group_code, " - ", group_name, "<br>",
  "<b>Subgroup:</b> ", subgroup_code, " - ", subgroup_name
)

# Leaflet map
make_basemap() |>
  fitBounds(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]], bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymax"]]) |>
  addPolygons(
    data         = sf_oac,
    group        = "Supergroup",
    smoothFactor = 0.2,
    fillOpacity  = 0.5,
    fillColor    = ~pal_sg(supergroup_code),
    color        = "black",
    weight       = 0.4,
    popup        = popup_html
  ) |>
  addPolygons(
    data         = sf_oac,
    group        = "Group",
    smoothFactor = 0.2,
    fillOpacity  = 0.5,
    fillColor    = ~pal_grp(group_code),
    color        = "black",
    weight       = 0.4,
    popup        = popup_html
  ) |>
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Supergroup", "Group"),
    options    = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  ) |>
  hideGroup("Group") |>
  addLegend(
    position  = "topright",
    colors    = pal_sg(sg_lookup$supergroup_code),
    labels    = sg_lookup$label,
    opacity   = 0.6,
    title     = "Supergroup",
    className = "info legend legend-supergroup"
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    position  = "topright",
    colors    = pal_grp(grp_lookup$group_code),
    labels    = grp_lookup$label,
    opacity   = 0.6,
    title     = "Group",
    className = "info legend legend-group"
  ) |>
  htmlwidgets::onRender(sprintf("
    function(el, x) {
      var map = this;
      // Re-fit bounds with right padding to keep polygons clear of the legend
      map.fitBounds([[%f, %f], [%f, %f]], {paddingBottomRight: [260, 0]});
      // Hide group legend on load
      var grpLegend = document.querySelector('.legend-group');
      if (grpLegend) grpLegend.style.display = 'none';
      // Toggle legends when the base layer changes
      map.on('baselayerchange', function(e) {
        var sgLegend  = document.querySelector('.legend-supergroup');
        var grpLegend = document.querySelector('.legend-group');
        if (e.name === 'Supergroup') {
          if (sgLegend)  sgLegend.style.display  = 'block';
          if (grpLegend) grpLegend.style.display = 'none';
        } else {
          if (sgLegend)  sgLegend.style.display  = 'none';
          if (grpLegend) grpLegend.style.display = 'block';
        }
      });
    }
  ", bb[["ymin"]], bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymax"]], bb[["xmax"]]))

  # Remove zero-variance predictors
  step_zv(all_numeric_predictors()) |>

  # Impute any remaining missing values
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>

  # Standardise all predictors to mean = 0, sd = 1

  # Remove highly correlated variables
  step_corr(

  )
